Findings.Comment: The function's signature and documentation indicate the caller's context should bound the entire operation, including cancellation. However, the diff replaces uses of the passed `ctx` with `context.Background()` for both the HTTP request and the body read. This means the function no longer respects the caller's context, making the operation uncancellable and potentially causing resource leaks or hung operations if the parent context is cancelled.
Findings.Headline: Function ignores caller's context, uses background context instead
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)

Expected.why: NewRequestWithContext is handed context.Background() instead of ctx, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request.
getTextCapped is handed context.Background() too, so the body read is unbounded. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: The explicit `r.mu.Unlock()` is placed after the `t.Ready` and `r.disable` assignments, but the early-return path when the team is not found (`!ok`) skips the unlock. This leaves the mutex locked, causing a deadlock on the next call that acquires `r.mu`.
Findings.Headline: Deadlock on unknown team in Disable method
Findings.Suggestion:
r.mu.Unlock()
		return fmt.Errorf("unknown team %q", slug)
	}
	t.Ready = false
	r.disable[slug] = reason
	r.mu.Unlock()
	return nil

Findings.Comment: The explicit `r.mu.Unlock()` is placed after the `t.Ready` and `r.disable` assignments, but the early-return path when the team is not found (`!ok`) skips the unlock. This leaves the mutex locked, causing a deadlock on the next call that acquires `r.mu`.
Findings.Headline: Deadlock on unknown team in Disable method
Findings.Suggestion:
r.mu.Unlock()
		return fmt.Errorf("unknown team %q", slug)
	}
	t.Ready = false
	r.disable[slug] = reason
	r.mu.Unlock()
	return nil

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: When `r.Ticket` is `nil`, the guard was replaced with a no-op comment block, so execution falls through to `return r.Body + "\n\n" + r.Ticket.Key`. Dereferencing `Key` on a nil `*Ticket` panics at runtime. Every call to `Summarize` with a ticket-less `Result` (a case the original code explicitly handled) will crash.
Findings.Headline: Nil pointer dereference when Ticket is nil

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: When `last` is at or beyond the end of the file, the corrected code sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`, which is an out-of-bounds index for the slice. The subsequent slice `lines[first:last]` will panic. For example, with a 10-line file and a hunk starting at line 8 (`first=8`), requesting one context line sets `last=9`. The condition `last >= len(lines)` is true, so `last` becomes 11, causing a panic on the slice operation.
Findings.Headline: Index out of range in ContextAfter when hunk near end of file

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the end and panics instead of returning the available context.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` leaks the HTTP response body in all code paths where `c.http.Do(req)` returns a non-nil `resp`. When the status is non-2xx or JSON decoding fails, the function returns an error without closing the body. On the successful return, the caller gets a `*User` but the underlying response body remains open. In a server handling multiple requests, this leaks file descriptors and memory until the process restarts. Add `defer resp.Body.Close()` immediately after the error check on line 18.
Findings.Headline: Response body never closed — resource leak

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Updating `q.depth` without holding `q.mu` after `q.run(j)` creates a data race with `Depth()` (line 22) and `Submit()` (line 17), which read and write `q.depth` under the mutex. `Depth()` can be called concurrently and may read a stale or torn value while the worker modifies `q.depth`. Additionally, `len(q.pending)` is read without the mutex, racing with `Submit()` which appends to `q.pending` under the mutex.
Findings.Headline: Data race on depth and pending in worker after mutex removal — blocking

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The error returned by `tx.Commit(ctx)` is ignored, so if the commit fails (e.g., due to a deferred constraint violation or connection loss), the caller is falsely informed the claim was recorded. The deferred `tx.Rollback(ctx)` will clean up, but the method returns `nil`, causing silent data loss on commit failures.
Findings.Headline: Commit error ignored — silent data loss risk

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The `errNoRows` and generic-error branches have swapped their wrap targets. When `sql.ErrNoRows` fires (no claim exists), the returned error now wraps the raw `sql.ErrNoRows` instead of the public sentinel `ErrNoClaim`, so callers checking `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` get `false` — the documented contract is broken. Conversely, any other database fault (connection refused, timeout) now wraps `ErrNoClaim`, causing callers to treat a transient DB outage as "nobody owns this project." This inverts the distinguishability the docstring promises and can lead to incorrect ownership or access-control decisions during DB hiccups.
Findings.Headline: Wrap targets swapped between no-rows and generic-error paths

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
